01 / A DIFFERENT PERSPECTIVE本
What if eating wellmeant coming home?
Rice is more than a carbohydrate.It's a language of care.

Maybe you grew up hearing “Have you eaten?” when someone really meant “How are you?” On many Cantonese tables, care looks like a bowl of rice, a plate of greens, and soup kept warm for whoever gets home last. When familiar foods are suddenly labelled “bad,” eating can start to feel more anxious than nourishing.

You do not have to choose between looking after your health and keeping the food you love. Start with the whole meal: the vegetables you enjoy, a protein source, the grain portion that suits you, and the people you share it with. Small changes you can live with often make a better starting point than a long list of foods to fear.
02 / BEYOND THE LOW-CARB HEADLINE衡
Your roots matter.So does the evidence.
Low-carb advice can sound wonderfully simple. Real life is less tidy: family habits, medications, budget, and appetite all matter. Here is a little context to help you make sense of the headlines.
One diet doesn't fit all.

Some Asian populations develop type 2 diabetes at lower BMI levels, but that does not mean every Asian person needs the same diet. Family history, blood glucose, activity, and medical advice tell you more than the number on the scales alone. Rice can still have a place; the amount and the rest of the meal matter.
What you eat instead matters.

Eating less carbohydrate is only half the story—what takes its place? Cutting fruit, beans, and whole grains can make fibre harder to get. A meal with tofu, vegetables, and unsaturated fats is quite different from one built around processed meats, even if both are called “low-carb.”
Build a balanced plate.

For a practical starting point, picture roughly half a plate of vegetables, with the rest shared between protein and grains or other starches. At a shared family meal, you can build that balance in your own bowl. It is a flexible guide, not a test; adjust it with your clinician or dietitian if you have specific needs.

Low-carbohydrate diets may help some people manage blood glucose in the short term; long-term benefits, adherence, and food quality vary. This site does not claim that low-carb eating is uniquely harmful to all Asian people. If you take glucose-lowering medication, discuss major dietary changes with your clinician.

Lotus root & pork rib soup

When lotus root has had time to soften, its edges turn tender and the broth takes on a gentle sweetness. This is a familiar Cantonese pot to put on early and share slowly; serve the ribs and lotus root as well as the soup.
A little nourishment, explained
Pork provides protein, while eating the lotus root adds fibre and carbohydrate energy. Most of the protein stays in the meat, and bone broth should not be relied on as a calcium source.
A guide to energy per portion
About 275 kcal per serving (4 servings).
One quarter of the pot, including meat and lotus root; bones are not eaten. Assumes about 250 g edible pork from 450 g bone-in ribs.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
450 g pork ribs, cut into short pieces by the butcher
500 g lotus root, peeled and cut into thick slices
1.5 litres water, plus water for blanching
4 slices ginger
A little salt to taste
From the kitchen
Place ribs in a pot, cover with cold water and bring to a boil. Simmer for 3–5 minutes, then drain and discard this water. Clean the pot.
Add the blanched ribs, lotus root, ginger and 1.5 litres fresh water. Bring to a boil and skim off any foam.
Cover partly and simmer gently for 75–90 minutes, until the meat is thoroughly cooked and tender and the lotus root is soft. Add hot water if needed.
Taste before adding a little salt. Serve the solids with the broth; remove small bones carefully.
Serves 4 as a shared soup. No major allergens in the listed ingredients. Skim visible fat if you prefer a lighter broth.

Ginger & scallion steamed fish
A Cantonese classic that lets fresh ingredients speak. Gentle steaming, fragrant ginger, and plenty of greens make a simple shared plate.
A little nourishment, explained
Fish provides protein for maintaining muscles and repairing tissues. Steaming uses little added fat; serving it with vegetables and rice adds fibre and energy to round out the meal.
A guide to energy per portion
About 160 kcal per serving (2 servings).
One fillet with half the seasoning; excludes rice and vegetables suggested for serving.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
2 fish fillets (about 150 g each), thawed if frozen
15 g ginger, cut into fine strips
2 scallions, finely sliced
2 tsp reduced-sodium soy sauce
1 tsp sesame oil
Cooked brown rice and steamed greens, to serve
From the kitchen
Place fish on a heatproof plate and scatter with ginger.
Steam over simmering water for 8–12 minutes, depending on thickness, until the centre reaches 63°C and flakes easily.
Top with scallions, soy sauce, and sesame oil. Serve with rice and greens.
Serves 2. Contains fish, soy, sesame; soy sauce may contain wheat. Adjust grain portions to your needs.

Shiitake rice with fresh pork, cured pork or shrimp

Keep the fragrant mushrooms and rice, but leave out the tofu. Choose fresh pork for an everyday version, a little cured pork for a more traditional aroma, or shrimp when you fancy seafood; you do not need all three.
A little nourishment, explained

Rice supplies energy, while pork or shrimp adds protein and mushrooms contribute some fibre. Cured pork is salty processed meat, so use a small amount for flavour and choose fresh pork or shrimp more often.
A guide to energy per portion
About 480 kcal per serving (2 servings).
Fresh-pork option, half the rice recipe; excludes side vegetables. Cured-pork and shrimp options are listed separately.
Cured-pork option: about 525 kcal; shrimp option: 440 kcal per serving.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
150 g quick-cooking brown rice, or a white-and-brown rice blend; water as directed on the packet
150 g fresh shiitake mushrooms, sliced
Choose ONE: 150 g thinly sliced fresh lean pork; 60 g cured pork; or 150 g peeled raw shrimp
1 small onion, chopped; 10 g ginger, sliced
2 tsp vegetable oil; 1 tsp reduced-sodium soy sauce
Steamed greens to serve
From the kitchen
Cook the rice according to the packet. Keep it hot while preparing the topping.
If using cured pork, follow its package instructions to cook it fully before slicing. It is not automatically ready to eat.
Heat oil and cook onion, ginger and mushrooms for 5 minutes. Add fresh pork and cook fully to 71°C, or shrimp to 63°C and opaque throughout. For cooked cured pork, stir it in and heat thoroughly.
Fold the cooked topping into the hot rice. Add soy sauce gradually, especially when using salty cured pork.
Serve promptly with greens. Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate within 2 hours, and reheat until steaming hot.
Serves 2. Contains soy; soy sauce may contain wheat. Shrimp adds crustaceans; cured pork may have additional allergens. No tofu is used.

Mango & yoghurt cups
A quick fruit dessert inspired by Hong Kong mango sweets, with plain yoghurt instead of a sweetened cream base. A modern adaptation, not a traditional medicinal recipe.
A little nourishment, explained
Plain dairy yoghurt provides protein and calcium, which support normal bone health. Mango adds vitamin C and some fibre; using unsweetened yoghurt keeps added sugar lower than a sweetened version.
A guide to energy per portion
About 165 kcal per serving (2 servings).
One of two cups; assumes 200 g prepared mango and includes the optional nuts. Without nuts, about 135 kcal.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
1 ripe mango, peeled and diced
250 g plain unsweetened yoghurt
1 tsp lime juice
1 tbsp unsalted chopped pistachios (optional)
From the kitchen
Blend half the mango with the lime juice.
Layer yoghurt, mango purée, and remaining diced mango in two glasses.
Add optional nuts and serve immediately or refrigerate until serving.
Serves 2. Contains milk and optional pistachios. Fruit and yoghurt contain carbohydrates; adjust portions for your needs. Photo is a reference yoghurt dessert, not this exact recipe.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Coconut chicken soup
The appeal of coconut chicken is its clear, naturally sweet broth. Unsweetened coconut water and a little fresh coconut flesh do the work here; there is no need for coconut cream.
A little nourishment, explained

Chicken contributes protein, and the broth adds fluid. Coconut water still contains natural sugars and potassium, while coconut flesh contains saturated fat; enjoy a comfortable portion rather than treating the soup as a health tonic.
A guide to energy per portion
About 255 kcal per serving (4 servings).
One quarter of the pot including chicken, broth and coconut flesh; excludes bones and assumes skinless edible chicken.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
600 g bone-in chicken pieces
800 ml unsweetened coconut water
600 ml water
100 g fresh coconut flesh, thinly sliced
4 slices ginger; a little salt
From the kitchen
Place chicken in a pot with enough water to cover. Bring to a boil for 3 minutes, drain and discard the water, and clean the pot.
Add chicken, coconut water, 600 ml fresh water, coconut flesh and ginger. Bring just to a boil.
Lower the heat, partly cover and simmer for 45–55 minutes until chicken is tender and reaches 74°C in the thickest parts.
Season lightly. Serve the chicken with some broth and coconut flesh, watching for small bones.
Serves 4. Check packaged coconut water for added sugar. People advised to limit potassium should discuss coconut water with their clinician.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Winter melon, mushroom & tofu soup with optional shrimp and pork

Keep the original winter melon, mushrooms and tofu, then add a little fresh shrimp or sliced pork when you want a fuller flavour. The extra ingredients go in near the end, so the vegetables stay soft and the meat does not become tough.
A little nourishment, explained
Tofu adds plant protein; shrimp or lean pork can contribute more protein if included. The winter melon and mushrooms bring some fibre when eaten, while the broth contributes fluid.
A guide to energy per portion
About 75 kcal per serving (4 servings).
Base soup without meat or shrimp, one quarter of the pot. Optional additions change the energy.
With shrimp: about 105 kcal; with pork: 120 kcal; with both: 145 kcal per serving.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
400 g winter melon, peeled, deseeded and cubed
150 g fresh shiitake mushrooms, sliced
200 g firm tofu, cubed
Optional: 120 g peeled raw shrimp and/or 120 g thinly sliced lean pork
1 litre water; 3 slices ginger; 1 tsp vegetable oil
A little salt and white pepper
From the kitchen
Warm oil in a pot and cook ginger and mushrooms for 3 minutes.
Add winter melon and water, bring to a boil and simmer for 20 minutes.
Add tofu. If using pork, add the slices now and simmer for 6–8 minutes until fully cooked; thin slices should reach 71°C for a simple home-kitchen safety target.

If using shrimp, add them near the end, whether or not pork was added, and simmer for 3–5 minutes until opaque throughout and at least 63°C. Without meat or shrimp, simply heat the tofu through for 5 minutes.
Season lightly and serve all the ingredients with the broth.
Serves 4 as a side. Contains soy; optional shrimp adds crustaceans. Keep raw seafood or pork separate from ready-to-eat foods.

Silky steamed eggs with mushrooms

If steamed eggs remind you of dinner at home, you are in good company. The trick is gentle heat and a little patience: cover the bowl, keep the water at a simmer, and let the eggs settle into a soft custard.
A little nourishment, explained
Eggs provide protein and choline, a nutrient involved in normal cell function. Add greens and a serving of rice to bring fibre and carbohydrate energy to the meal.
A guide to energy per portion
About 95 kcal per serving (3 servings).
One third of the shared egg dish; excludes rice and other sides.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
3 eggs
300 ml lukewarm water
80 g fresh shiitake mushrooms, finely sliced
1 tsp reduced-sodium soy sauce
1 tsp sesame oil; 1 scallion, sliced
From the kitchen
Beat the eggs gently with the water, then strain into a shallow heatproof bowl. Skim off bubbles.
Scatter over the thinly sliced mushrooms and cover with a heatproof plate or foil.
Steam over gently simmering water for about 15–18 minutes, until the centre is set and reaches 71°C. Add time if needed.
Remove carefully, uncover, and add soy sauce, sesame oil, and scallions. Serve with rice and greens.
Serves 3 as a shared dish. Contains egg, soy and sesame; soy sauce may contain wheat. Steam until fully cooked, especially for young children and pregnant people.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Seafood clay-pot congee

A good pot of seafood congee starts with rice that has had time to bloom. Add the seafood only when the base is creamy, so the prawns stay tender and the fish does not disappear; a heavy saucepan works if you do not have a clay pot.
A little nourishment, explained
Fish and prawns provide protein, while rice contributes easy-to-eat carbohydrate energy. Congee is not inherently low in carbohydrate; a side of cooked vegetables helps add fibre and variety.
A guide to energy per portion
About 250 kcal per serving (3 servings).
One third of the congee, made with water rather than a rich stock; no extra side dishes.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
120 g white rice, rinsed
1.5 litres water or unsalted fish stock
150 g peeled raw prawns
150 g boneless white fish, sliced
15 g ginger, finely shredded
1 tsp sesame oil; chopped scallion; a little salt and white pepper
From the kitchen
Use a food-safe clay pot suitable for your hob, or a heavy saucepan. Bring rice and water to a boil, stirring so grains do not stick.
Simmer partly covered for 40–45 minutes, stirring often and adding hot water if needed, until the rice opens and the congee thickens.
Add ginger, prawns and fish. Simmer gently for about 5–8 minutes, until all seafood is opaque and reaches at least 63°C.
Season lightly, finish with scallion and sesame oil, and serve hot. Check carefully for fish bones.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and reheat until steaming throughout; do not leave congee sitting warm for hours.
Serves 3. Contains fish, crustaceans and sesame; check stock for other allergens. Texture can be soft without making it a treatment for digestive illness.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Red bean & tangerine peel soup

There is something lovely about ending a meal with a small bowl of warm tong sui. This version lets the beans do most of the talking; a little tangerine peel adds the familiar citrus note without needing much sugar.
A little nourishment, explained

Adzuki beans provide fibre and plant protein, so the beans themselves offer more than sweetness. Keeping some beans whole and adding only a little sugar helps preserve the character of this traditional dessert.
A guide to energy per portion
About 140 kcal per serving (4 servings).
One of four bowls, using 15 g sugar in the pot and eating the beans, not just the liquid.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
150 g dried adzuki beans, rinsed
1 small piece dried tangerine peel (about 2 g), rinsed
1.2 litres water, plus more if needed
10–20 g sugar, to taste
From the kitchen
Soak the beans for 8 hours or overnight in the refrigerator, then drain. The soaking time is extra.
Put beans, tangerine peel, and fresh water in a pot. Bring to a full boil for 10 minutes.
Reduce the heat and simmer for 60–80 minutes, stirring occasionally and adding hot water if needed, until very soft.
Remove the peel if preferred. Mash some beans for a thicker texture, then add sugar a little at a time. Serve in small bowls.
Serves 4. Beans and added sugar both contribute carbohydrates. Keep portions comfortable for you; this is a dessert, not a treatment for any condition.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Rock sugar steamed snow pear

Keep the pear pieces generous and the sweetness gentle. Slow steaming gives the fruit time to soften, making this a lovely warm dessert without needing to turn it into a promise about coughs or colds.
A little nourishment, explained
Eating the pear provides fibre that supports normal bowel function. Rock sugar is still added sugar, not a healthier medicine-like form of sweetener, so use only what the dessert needs.
A guide to energy per portion
About 95 kcal per serving (3 servings).
Three small bowls including pear and all the sweetened liquid; about 145 kcal each if divided into two larger bowls.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
2 snow pears, washed, cored and cut into large pieces
10–15 g rock sugar, adjusted to taste
350 ml drinking water
A heatproof lidded bowl and a steamer
From the kitchen
Peel the pears if preferred, or keep the washed skin for more texture.
Place pear, water and rock sugar in a heatproof lidded bowl. Cover the bowl.
Steam over gently boiling water for 35–45 minutes, until the pears are tender. Check the steamer water and top up safely if needed.
Let cool to a comfortable temperature and serve the fruit with its liquid.
Serves 2–3. No major allergens in the listed ingredients. This dessert does not treat coughs or respiratory illness.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Sweetcorn, carrot & pork rib soup
The sweetness here comes from corn and carrots, not a spoonful of sugar. It is a reassuring family soup: the kind you can leave gently bubbling while the rest of dinner comes together.
A little nourishment, explained
Pork supplies protein, carrots provide beta-carotene, and corn contributes fibre and carbohydrate energy. Eating the ingredients gives you more of these nutrients than drinking only the clear soup.
A guide to energy per portion
About 240 kcal per serving (4 servings).
One quarter of the pot, with meat, carrot and edible corn kernels; bones and corn cobs excluded.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
450 g pork ribs, cut into short pieces
1 large corn cob, cut into sections
2 carrots (about 250 g), cut into chunks
1.5 litres water, plus blanching water
4 slices ginger; a little salt
From the kitchen
Cover ribs with cold water, bring to a boil and blanch for 3–5 minutes. Drain and discard the water; clean the pot.
Put ribs, corn, carrots and ginger in the pot with 1.5 litres fresh water. Bring to a boil.
Reduce to a gentle simmer, partly cover and cook for 70–80 minutes, until ribs are fully cooked and tender.
Skim excess fat if desired, season lightly and serve the meat and vegetables with the soup.
Serves 4. No major allergens in the listed ingredients. Corn is also a starchy food; adjust the rest of the meal to your appetite.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Watercress & chicken soup
The peppery smell of watercress is part of the pleasure of this familiar soup. Let the chicken simmer gently, then add the greens toward the end so they keep a little of their character.
A little nourishment, explained

Chicken provides protein for maintaining muscles and repairing tissues. Watercress contributes vitamin K, which supports normal blood clotting; people taking warfarin should keep vitamin K intake consistent with clinical advice.
A guide to energy per portion
About 125 kcal per serving (4 servings).
One quarter of the pot including the chicken and vegetables, not broth alone.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
300 g boneless skinless chicken thigh, cut into large pieces
250 g watercress, trimmed and washed thoroughly
1 carrot, sliced
1.2 litres water; 4 slices ginger
A little salt to taste
From the kitchen
Keep raw chicken separate from ready-to-eat foods; wash hands and utensils after handling it.
Bring water and ginger to a boil. Add chicken and carrot, return to a simmer and cook for 30 minutes.
Add watercress and simmer for 10 minutes. Check the chicken reaches 74°C throughout.
Season lightly. Serve the chicken and greens along with the broth.
Serves 4 as a side. No major allergens in the listed ingredients; check any added seasoning. This soup is not a remedy for respiratory illness.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Papaya & pork rib soup
Use firm, just-ripe papaya so it softens without disappearing into the pot. This version leaves out peanuts and tofu and keeps the familiar pairing of papaya, ginger and pork ribs.
A little nourishment, explained
Pork provides protein, and the papaya flesh contributes fibre and carotenoids. Enjoy the fruit as well as the broth; this soup is not proven to increase breast milk or change body shape.
A guide to energy per portion
About 235 kcal per serving (4 servings).
One quarter of the pot, including meat and papaya; assumes 250 g edible pork.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
450 g pork ribs, cut into short pieces
500 g firm just-ripe papaya, peeled, deseeded and cut into large chunks
1.5 litres water, plus blanching water
4 slices ginger; a little salt
From the kitchen
Blanch the ribs in water brought from cold to a boil for 3–5 minutes. Drain, discard the water and clean the pot.
Bring ribs, ginger and 1.5 litres fresh water to a boil, then simmer for 45 minutes.
Add papaya and simmer gently for 30–35 minutes, until the pork is fully cooked and tender and the fruit is soft.
Taste, season lightly and serve carefully around the bones.
Serves 4. Avoid if allergic to papaya. No peanuts are used in this version.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Chinese olive & pork rib soup
Fresh Chinese olives give this soup a gently astringent edge followed by a mellow finish. Use the green fruit sold for Chinese soup-making, not brined Mediterranean table olives.
A little nourishment, explained
The pork is the main source of protein here; the broth contributes fluid. Chinese olives are used for flavour and tradition, not as a proven treatment for sore throats or other illnesses.
A guide to energy per portion
About 200 kcal per serving (4 servings).
One quarter of the pot, including pork; olive stones and bones excluded. Olive size and how much flesh is eaten vary.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
450 g pork ribs, cut into short pieces
6–8 fresh Chinese green olives (Canarium album), washed and lightly cracked
1.5 litres water, plus blanching water
4 slices ginger; a little salt
From the kitchen
Blanch ribs from cold water to a boil for 3–5 minutes, then drain and discard the water. Clean the pot.
Place ribs, cracked olives and ginger in the pot with fresh water. Bring to a boil.
Partly cover and simmer for 90 minutes, until the ribs are fully cooked and tender.
Season lightly. Remove olive stones and any bone fragments before eating; do not bite down on the stones.
Serves 4. No major allergens in the listed ingredients. Fresh Chinese olives contain hard stones; supervise children carefully.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Cordyceps flower & chicken soup

A handful of golden cordyceps flowers gives this chicken soup its familiar colour and earthy aroma. Buy cultivated, food-grade cordyceps flowers from a reputable food supplier; this is a family soup, not a medicinal preparation.
A little nourishment, explained
Chicken provides protein for maintaining muscles and repairing tissues. The mushrooms add flavour, but this soup should not be described as boosting immunity or treating lung or kidney conditions.
A guide to energy per portion
About 125 kcal per serving (4 servings).
One quarter of the pot including chicken and fungi; assumes about 300 g edible skinless chicken from the bone-in pieces.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
500 g bone-in chicken pieces
20 g dried food-grade cultivated cordyceps flowers (Cordyceps militaris)
1.5 litres water, plus blanching water
4 slices ginger; a little salt
From the kitchen
Rinse cordyceps flowers and soak briefly for 10 minutes in clean water, then drain. Follow any additional preparation advice on the packet.
Put chicken in a pot, cover with water and bring to a boil for 3 minutes. Drain and discard this water; clean the pot and utensils.
Bring chicken, ginger, cordyceps flowers and fresh water to a boil, then simmer gently for 60–70 minutes.
Check the thickest chicken pieces reach at least 74°C, season lightly and serve. Remove small bones carefully.
Serves 4. Avoid if allergic to mushrooms. Use food-grade ingredients, not supplement extracts or wild-foraged fungi.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Easy scallion-oil chicken thighs

Boneless thighs make this a much more manageable weekday dish than a whole chicken. Steam them first, then spoon over a small pan of warm scallion oil—the kitchen smells wonderful, and there is no need to handle a large pot of hot oil.
A little nourishment, explained

Chicken provides protein for maintaining muscle and repairing tissues. Using a modest amount of scallion oil keeps the aroma without making the dish excessively oily; removing skin also reduces some fat.
A guide to energy per portion
About 370 kcal per serving (2 servings).
One thigh with half the scallion oil, using boneless skinless chicken; excludes rice and greens. Skin-on thighs can be appreciably higher.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
2 boneless chicken thighs, about 400 g total
4 scallions, finely sliced; 15 g ginger, finely chopped
1 tbsp vegetable oil
2 tsp reduced-sodium soy sauce
2 tbsp hot chicken cooking juices; a little salt if needed
From the kitchen
Place thighs in a shallow heatproof dish. Steam over boiling water for 18–25 minutes, depending on thickness, until the centre of every thigh reaches 74°C.
Rest for 3–5 minutes, then slice on a clean board. Reserve 2 tbsp hot cooking juices.
Warm oil in a small pan over medium-low heat. Add ginger and scallions and stir for 1–2 minutes until fragrant, without burning them.
Turn the heat low and carefully stir in soy sauce and hot chicken juices. Bring to a brief simmer, then spoon over the chicken.
Serve with rice and a generous side of greens.
Serves 2. Contains soy; soy sauce may contain wheat. No shrimp or tofu is used in this version.

Garlic stir-fried sweet potato leaves
Choose tender leaves and soft young stems, and take a moment to pick away the tough bits. Once that is done, garlic and a hot wok are almost all this familiar southern Chinese vegetable needs.
A little nourishment, explained
Sweet potato leaves contribute fibre, folate and carotenoids. Their vitamin K content also matters for people taking warfarin, who should keep intake consistent with clinical advice.
A guide to energy per portion
About 90 kcal per serving (3 servings).
One third of the vegetable side, including oil; excludes rice.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
400 g edible sweet potato leaves and tender stems from a food supplier
4 garlic cloves, finely chopped
2 tsp vegetable oil
2–3 tbsp water; a little salt
From the kitchen
Pick away tough stems, wash the leaves thoroughly and drain. Use identified edible leaves, not ornamental plants.
Heat oil in a wok and stir-fry garlic briefly for about 20 seconds, without browning it too much.
Add stems first, then leaves. Stir-fry, add water, cover for 1–2 minutes and cook until stems are tender and leaves are fully wilted.
Uncover, season lightly and toss. Serve hot alongside rice and a protein dish.
Serves 2–3 as a side. No major allergens in the listed ingredients. This is a vegetable dish and contains no beef.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Simply stir-fried lettuce
Lettuce does not always have to be a salad. A quick turn in a hot wok softens the leaves while the ribs keep a little crunch; cook it just before everyone sits down.
A little nourishment, explained
Lettuce adds vegetables, some fibre and folate to the meal. This is a vegetable side dish, so pair it with a protein food and a grain rather than expecting it to supply everything on its own.
A guide to energy per portion
About 50 kcal per serving (3 servings).
One third of the vegetable side, including its share of oil.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
400 g fresh lettuce, leaves separated, washed and thoroughly drained
2 garlic cloves, lightly crushed (optional)
2 tsp vegetable oil
A small pinch of salt; 1–2 tbsp water if needed
From the kitchen
Cut large leaves into manageable pieces and make sure excess washing water has drained away.
Heat a wok over medium-high heat. Add oil and optional garlic and stir for about 20 seconds.
Add lettuce in batches and stir-fry for 1–2 minutes until just wilted; add a splash of water only if it catches.
Season lightly and serve straight away. No oyster sauce is needed for this simple version.
Serves 2–3 as a side. No major allergens in the listed ingredients. No tofu or oyster sauce is used.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Tomato & scrambled eggs: sweet or savoury

Every family seems to have its own tomato eggs. Some southern households prefer a little sweetness, while many northern versions lean savoury—but tastes overlap everywhere, so make the version your family enjoys.
A little nourishment, explained

Eggs provide protein and choline, while tomatoes add carotenoids and some vitamin C. The choice of sweet or savoury mainly changes added sugar or sodium, not whether the dish can belong in a balanced meal.
A guide to energy per portion
About 190 kcal per serving (2 servings).
Savoury version, half the dish; no rice or added sugar.
Adding 1–2 tsp sugar to the whole pan adds about 10–15 kcal per serving.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
3 eggs, beaten
3 ripe tomatoes (about 400 g), cut into wedges
2 tsp vegetable oil, divided
2 tbsp water; 1 scallion, sliced
Savoury option: a small pinch of salt, or 1 tsp reduced-sodium soy sauce
Sweeter option: add 1–2 tsp sugar to the tomato sauce, to taste
From the kitchen
Heat 1 tsp oil and scramble the eggs until just set. Transfer to a clean plate.
Add remaining oil and tomatoes. Cook for 5–7 minutes, pressing gently to release juice, and add water if needed.
For a sweeter version, stir in sugar a little at a time. For a savoury version, use a little salt or soy sauce instead; neither version needs heavy seasoning.
Return eggs and stir until thoroughly hot and the egg mixture reaches 71°C.
Scatter with scallions and serve with rice. Taste before adding anything else.
Serves 2. Contains egg; the soy-sauce option adds soy and may add wheat. Regional preferences are examples, not rules for all northern or southern families.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Cantonese sweet & sour pork
Crisp pork, juicy pineapple and a glossy sweet-and-sour sauce make this a proper Cantonese treat. Fry in small batches and toss with the sauce right at the end, so the coating keeps a little crunch.
A little nourishment, explained

Pork provides protein and B vitamins, and peppers and pineapple add some plant nutrients. This is a fried dish with added sugar and sodium, so enjoy a moderate portion alongside plenty of vegetables rather than presenting it as a health food.
A guide to energy per portion
About 445 kcal per serving (3 servings).
One third of the dish, excluding rice. Approximation assumes 30 g oil is retained overall; the amount absorbed during frying is uncertain.
Allow a broad range of roughly 420–560 kcal per serving, depending on pork cut, coating and oil absorption.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
300 g pork shoulder or loin, cut into 2 cm pieces
1 egg, beaten; 1 tsp reduced-sodium soy sauce
50–70 g cornflour for coating
150 g pineapple chunks; 1 sweet pepper and half an onion, cut into chunks
Sauce: 3 tbsp ketchup, 2 tbsp rice vinegar, 1 tbsp sugar, 4 tbsp water
1 tsp cornflour mixed with 1 tbsp water
Vegetable oil for shallow-frying, about 1 cm deep; 1 tsp extra for the sauce
From the kitchen
Mix pork with soy sauce and enough beaten egg to coat lightly. Refrigerate for 10 minutes, then coat well with cornflour. Discard unused raw egg mixture.
Heat about 1 cm oil in a stable deep-sided pan to about 170–175°C. Fry pork in small batches, turning carefully, until golden and cooked to at least 71°C in the centre. Drain on a rack.
Mix ketchup, vinegar, sugar and water. In a separate pan, heat 1 tsp oil and stir-fry onion and pepper for 2–3 minutes.
Add pineapple and sauce, bring to a simmer, then add cornflour water and stir until glossy.
Add fried pork only at the end, toss briefly and serve immediately with rice and vegetables. Keep water away from hot frying oil.
Serves 3 as a shared dish. Contains egg and soy; check ketchup and soy sauce for wheat or other allergens. Never leave frying oil unattended.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Stir-fried gai lan & beef

Tender beef and crisp gai lan are a Cantonese restaurant pairing that works beautifully at home. Slice the stems thinly and give them a head start in the wok, so the leaves do not overcook while you wait.
A little nourishment, explained
Beef provides protein and readily absorbed haem iron for normal red blood cell formation. Gai lan contributes fibre, folate and vitamin K, giving the plate more variety than meat alone.
A guide to energy per portion
About 350 kcal per serving (2 servings).
Half the beef and vegetables, including sauce; excludes the rice served alongside.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
250 g beef steak, thinly sliced across the grain
350 g gai lan (Chinese broccoli), washed; stems sliced thinly
10 g ginger, sliced; 2 tsp vegetable oil
Marinade: 1 tsp reduced-sodium soy sauce, 1 tsp cornflour, 1 tbsp water
Sauce: 1 tsp oyster sauce and 2 tbsp water; optional, or use a little soy sauce instead
From the kitchen
Mix beef with marinade and refrigerate for 10 minutes while preparing the vegetables.
Heat 1 tsp oil, add ginger and gai lan stems, then leaves and a splash of water. Stir-fry until tender-crisp; transfer to a clean plate.
Heat the remaining oil and spread beef in a thin layer. Cook in batches until it reaches at least 63°C, then keep hot for at least 3 minutes before serving; cook further if preferred.
Return gai lan, add the sauce and toss until everything is hot and lightly coated.
Serve promptly with rice and enjoy the gai lan while it is still crisp.
Serves 2. Contains soy; oyster sauce contains molluscs and sauces may contain wheat. People taking warfarin should keep leafy-green intake consistent with medical advice.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Double-skin milk pudding

The two delicate milk skins are what give this Shunde dessert its name. Use full-fat milk, let the first skin form patiently, and pour slowly so it stays in the bowl; it is a small kitchen ritual worth taking your time over.
A little nourishment, explained

Milk contributes protein and calcium for normal bone health, while egg white adds protein. This is a sweetened dairy dessert with saturated fat, so enjoy a small bowl rather than expecting extra health benefits from the milk skins.
A guide to energy per portion
About 185 kcal per serving (2 servings).
One of two bowls, using full-fat milk and 22.5 g sugar in the whole recipe.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
400 ml pasteurised full-fat milk
2 egg whites, about 60 g total
20–25 g sugar, adjusted to taste
2 small heatproof bowls; fine sieve
From the kitchen
Warm milk in a small saucepan until steaming but not vigorously boiling. Divide between two bowls and let stand for 10–15 minutes until a skin forms.
Carefully lift one edge of each skin and pour most of the milk back into a jug, leaving the skin and a little milk in each bowl.
Let the poured milk cool until lukewarm. Gently mix in sugar and egg whites without whipping in air, then strain.
Pour the mixture slowly down the side of each bowl so the first skin floats up. Cover each bowl with a heatproof plate or foil.
Steam over gently simmering water for 12–18 minutes until just set and at least 71°C in the centre; leave covered off the heat for 3 minutes. Cool slightly before serving.
Serves 2. Contains milk and egg. Use pasteurised milk and cook fully; an under-set raw egg centre is not the goal.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Mango pomelo sago

Juicy mango, little pearls of sago and a few spoonfuls of pomelo make this a familiar Hong Kong sweet. This version uses the traditional sago rather than chia seeds; keep the fruit flavour in front and taste before adding sugar.
A little nourishment, explained

Mango and pomelo provide vitamin C, and the milk or fortified soy drink can contribute protein and calcium. Sago supplies starch, and coconut milk contains saturated fat; this is a dessert to portion, not a low-carb fruit drink.
A guide to energy per portion
About 225 kcal per serving (4 servings).
One of four small bowls, using canned coconut milk, dairy milk and 5 g optional sugar. Lighter coconut drinks give a different result.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
2 ripe mangoes, about 400 g prepared flesh
40 g small sago pearls
100 g pomelo flesh, membranes removed
150 ml unsweetened coconut milk
200 ml pasteurised milk or unsweetened fortified soy drink
0–10 g sugar, optional; plenty of water for boiling sago
From the kitchen
Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Add sago, stir and boil following the packet, commonly 10–15 minutes, until only tiny white centres remain.
Turn off the heat, cover for 10 minutes or as directed, until translucent. If centres remain chalky, briefly boil again. Drain and rinse with drinking water to cool.
Blend half the mango with coconut milk and milk or soy drink. Dice the remaining mango.
Fold in cooled sago and mango pieces. Taste before adding optional sugar, then top with pomelo.
Refrigerate promptly until cold and serve the same day if possible. Do not leave cooked sago warm on the counter.

Serves 4 small bowls. Contains milk or soy depending on the choice; check coconut milk for other allergens. Pomelo can interact with some medicines—ask a pharmacist if you have been advised to avoid grapefruit or pomelo.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Traditional black sesame paste

Toasty sesame and a smooth, spoonable texture are the heart of this classic tong sui. A little rice helps it thicken in the traditional way; stir patiently over a low heat so the bottom does not catch.
A little nourishment, explained
Sesame provides unsaturated fats and some protein, and the rice adds carbohydrate energy. Sesame paste is energy-dense even with little sugar; it does not prevent grey hair or treat illness.
A guide to energy per portion
About 170 kcal per serving (3 servings).
One of three small bowls, including 20 g sugar in the whole recipe.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
60 g roasted black sesame seeds
25 g white rice, soaked in the refrigerator for 2 hours, then drained
550 ml drinking water, plus a little more if needed
15–25 g sugar, adjusted to taste
From the kitchen
If sesame is not already roasted, toast in a dry pan over low heat until fragrant, without burning, then cool. Soaking time for the rice is extra.
Blend sesame, drained rice and water thoroughly. Use a fine sieve if you prefer a very smooth paste.
Pour into a heavy saucepan and bring to a gentle simmer, stirring continuously.
Cook for 12–15 minutes until the rice is fully cooked and the paste thickens. Thin with hot water if needed, and add sugar gradually.
Divide into small bowls and let cool slightly before eating.
Serves 3. Contains sesame. No mung beans or coconut milk are used in this version.
Photograph supplied in the owner’s edited website; preserved unchanged.
Steamed papaya with fresh milk

Rather than boiling everything together, let the papaya and milk warm gently in a covered bowl over water. Choose a ripe but firm papaya and keep the sweetness light; this is a quiet, simple dessert to finish dinner.
A little nourishment, explained

Milk provides protein and calcium for normal bone health, while the papaya flesh adds some fibre and carotenoids. It is a nourishing dessert, not a way to increase breast milk, change body shape or treat illness.
A guide to energy per portion
About 175 kcal per serving (2 servings).
One of two bowls, using full-fat milk and 10 g optional rock sugar in total.
A rough ingredient-based kitchen estimate, not a measured nutrition value. Meat yield, oil, brands and portion size will change it.
Ingredients
300 g ripe but firm papaya, peeled, deseeded and cubed
300 ml pasteurised milk
5–10 g rock sugar, optional
2 small heatproof lidded bowls; a steamer
From the kitchen
Divide the papaya between two heatproof bowls. Add milk and optional rock sugar, leaving space at the top.
Cover each bowl. Place in a steamer over gently boiling water.
Steam for 20–25 minutes until the papaya is tender and the milk is hot throughout; do not let the steamer run dry.
Let stand for 3–5 minutes and serve warm. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and use within 2 days.
Serves 2. Contains milk. Use lactose-free milk if needed; avoid papaya if allergic. Mild curdling can occur with papaya, so serve soon after cooking.

好好食飯 · THE ART OF EATING WELL
各樣一點，滋養日常。食有度，養有道。
01 / 換一個角度本
好好吃飯，也可以是回家的路。
米飯不只是碳水化合物。也是一種關懷的語言。
你可能也聽慣了那句「食咗飯未？」——有時問的，其實是「你今日好嗎？」。在不少廣東家庭，關心就是一碗飯、一碟菜，還有留給最晚回家那個人的一鍋暖湯。當熟悉的食物忽然被貼上「不好」的標籤，吃飯便可能多了焦慮，少了自在。
照顧健康，不代表一定要放棄自己喜歡的食物。不妨先看看整餐：有沒有喜歡的蔬菜、合適的蛋白質食物、適合自己的飯量，以及能一起吃飯的人。從做得到的小調整開始，往往比記住一長串「不能吃」更容易走下去。
02 / 低碳標題以外衡
尊重飲食根源。也尊重科學證據。
低碳飲食的建議聽起來有時很簡單，但生活沒那麼整齊：家人的習慣、用藥、預算和食慾，都會影響選擇。先多了解一點背景，再看那些標題，或許就沒那麼迷惘。
沒有人人適用的餐單。
部分亞洲族群在較低 BMI 下也可能出現第二型糖尿病，但不代表每個亞洲人都需要同一份餐單。家族病史、血糖、活動量和醫護評估，比單看體重更有幫助。米飯仍可以留在餐桌上，份量和整餐配搭同樣重要。
用甚麼替代碳水很重要。
少吃碳水化合物，只說了故事的一半——騰出來的位置由甚麼填上？如果連水果、豆類和全穀物都減少了，纖維就可能不夠。以豆腐、蔬菜和不飽和脂肪為主的一餐，與依賴加工肉類的一餐，即使都叫「低碳」，也很不一樣。
從均衡的一餐開始。
可以先想像一個簡單比例：約半碟是蔬菜，其餘分給蛋白質食物、穀物或其他澱粉類。在一起夾菜的家常飯局，也可以在自己的碗裡慢慢配搭。這只是有彈性的起點，不是考試；有特別需要時，可與醫生或營養師一起調整。
低碳及極低碳飲食可能幫助部分人短期控制血糖；長期效益、持續實行的可行性和食物品質則各有不同。本站不主張低碳飲食對所有亞洲人都有獨特危害。如正在服用降血糖藥物，重大飲食改變前請諮詢醫護人員。

蓮藕排骨湯
蓮藕慢慢煲過，邊緣變軟，湯裡也多了一份清甜。這是廣東家裡很熟悉的一鍋湯，早一點煲起，晚飯時連排骨和蓮藕一起分著吃。
這一餐，怎樣滋養身體？
排骨提供蛋白質，吃下蓮藕也可攝取纖維和碳水化合物能量。大部分蛋白質仍在肉裡，骨湯也不宜當成主要補鈣來源。
每份熱量參考
每份約 275 千卡（全份分 4 份）。
按一鍋分 4 份、連肉和蓮藕計，骨不計食用；假設 450 克帶骨排骨約有 250 克可食肉。
按食材估算的家常參考，並非實測營養數值；可食肉量、用油、品牌和實際份量都會影響結果。
食材
排骨 450 克，請肉販斬件
蓮藕 500 克，去皮切厚片
清水 1.5 公升，另備汆水用水
薑 4 片
少量鹽調味
做法

01 / 换一个角度本
好好吃饭，也可以是回家的路。
米饭不只是碳水化合物。也是一种关怀的语言。
你可能也听惯了那句「食咗饭未？」——有时问的，其实是「你今日好吗？」。在不少广东家庭，关心就是一碗饭、一碟菜，还有留给最晚回家那个人的一锅暖汤。当熟悉的食物忽然被贴上「不好」的标签，吃饭便可能多了焦虑，少了自在。
照顾健康，不代表一定要放弃自己喜欢的食物。不妨先看看整餐：有没有喜欢的蔬菜、合适的蛋白质食物、适合自己的饭量，以及能一起吃饭的人。从做得到的小调整开始，往往比记住一长串「不能吃」更容易走下去。
02 / 低碳标题以外衡
尊重饮食根源。也尊重科学证据。
低碳饮食的建议听起来有时很简单，但生活没那么整齐：家人的习惯、用药、预算和食欲，都会影响选择。先多了解一点背景，再看那些标题，或许就没那么迷惘。
没有人人适用的餐单。
部分亚洲族群在较低 BMI 下也可能出现第二型糖尿病，但不代表每个亚洲人都需要同一份餐单。家族病史、血糖、活动量和医护评估，比单看体重更有帮助。米饭仍可以留在餐桌上，份量和整餐配搭同样重要。
用什么替代碳水很重要。
少吃碳水化合物，只说了故事的一半——腾出来的位置由甚么填上？如果连水果、豆类和全谷物都减少了，纤维就可能不够。以豆腐、蔬菜和不饱和脂肪为主的一餐，与依赖加工肉类的一餐，即使都叫「低碳」，也很不一样。
从均衡的一餐开始。
可以先想像一个简单比例：约半碟是蔬菜，其余分给蛋白质食物、谷物或其他淀粉类。在一起夹菜的家常饭局，也可以在自己的碗里慢慢配搭。这只是有弹性的起点，不是考试；有特别需要时，可与医生或营养师一起调整。
低碳及极低碳饮食可能帮助部分人短期控制血糖；长期效益、持续实行的可行性和食物品质则各有不同。本站不主张低碳饮食对所有亚洲人都有独特危害。如正在服用降血糖药物，重大饮食改变前请咨询医护人员。

莲藕排骨汤
莲藕慢慢煲过，边缘变软，汤里也多了一份清甜。这是广东家里很熟悉的一锅汤，早一点煲起，晚饭时连排骨和莲藕一起分著吃。
这一餐，怎样滋养身体？
排骨提供蛋白质，吃下莲藕也可摄取纤维和碳水化合物能量。大部分蛋白质仍在肉里，骨汤也不宜当成主要补钙来源。

做法
排骨放入锅中，加冷水盖过，煮沸后汆 3–5 分钟，沥干并倒去汆水，清洁锅子。
放回排骨，加入莲藕、姜和 1.5 公升新清水，煮沸并撇去浮沫。
半盖锅盖，小火煲 75–90 分钟，至排骨熟透软身、莲藕软熟；有需要可加热水。
先试味，再加少量盐。汤料和汤一起享用，小心碎骨。

芝麻糊
炒香芝麻的香气，配上滑滑又挂匙的质地，就是经典芝麻糊。用少量米帮助变稠，是很家常的传统做法；小火耐心搅，就不易黏底。
这一餐，怎样滋养身体？
芝麻提供不饱和脂肪和一些蛋白质，米则加上碳水化合物能量。即使少糖，芝麻糊仍是能量较密集的甜品，也不能预防白发或治疗疾病。

做法
木瓜分入两个耐热炖盅，倒入牛奶，加可选冰糖，盅顶留少量空间。
盖好盅盖，放入水微滚的蒸锅。
隔水炖 20–25 分钟，至木瓜软熟、牛奶全热，留意蒸锅不要烧干。
